account: For D8/D13, I derived three design constraints, each labeled design inference, mapping Dung's extension semantics to contradiction handling and belief revision in the many-to-many Q/A graph. The only dossier content I can cite is the single workspace file, papers/text/dung-1995-argumentation.txt, which provides the definitions (preferred, grounded, stable extensions; admissible/acceptable; characteristic function; semantic coincidence conditions). I explicitly separate the observed definitions from my design inferences. Counterevidence I noticed: (a) the source does not mention belief revision or answer graphs, so any such mapping is inference; (b) the source warns that stable extensions may not exist and that preferred extensions may not be unique, so the design must treat these as failure/variability modes; (c) the source warns that general extension computation is incomputable (page 25), so the design must bound the argument set to stay tractable. Sufficiency is partial because I only have the Dung file in hand and cannot support the broader synthesis, but for this node's design-inference deliverable the source is adequate.
assumptions: I assume that the parent will synthesize the design constraints into the final memo, respecting the explicit 'design inference' labeling.

I assume that the many-to-many Q/A graph can be projected onto an argumentation framework by treating each answer as an argument and each conflict edge as an attack edge; provenance edges (e.g., answer-addresses-question) are treated as non-attack relations and do not enter the attack graph.
I assume that a revision operation is a single transaction that atomically updates the attack/argument set and triggers a recomputation of the relevant extensions.

boundary_findings.alternative_explanation: The source may implicitly support revision by its treatment of nonmonotonic reasoning, but that is not stated explicitly.
boundary_findings.consequence_if_absorbed: If the final memo claims that Dung's semantics 'define' belief revision (rather than that they are a useful formalism for it), it would violate D13 (source-supported vs design inference) and overstate the source.
evidence: No occurrence of 'belief revision' in the provided Dung text.
Definition 2 defines only (AR, attacks); no graph or Q/A structures.
Theorem 52 (PDF PAGE 25) warns of incomputability of general semantics.
boundary_findings.narrative: The node's objective assumes a many-to-many Q/A graph with 'contradiction and belief-revision behavior', but the only source provided (Dung) has no notion of belief revision, persistence, or graph substrate. The design constraints must therefore be pure inferences from the extension semantics, which is exactly what I have done. I have not observed any conflict or mismatch within the Dung file itself.
boundary_findings.smallest_suspected_scope: The design of belief-revision behavior in the overall substrate.

citations.excerpt: Definition 2. An argumentation framework is a pair AF=(AR,attacks) where AR is a set of arguments, and attacks is a binary relation on AR i.e. attacks ⊆ AR × AR

claims.statement: Dung defines an argumentation framework as a pair (AR, attacks) where AR is a set of arguments and attacks is a binary relation on AR; an argument is an abstract entity whose role is determined only by its relations to other arguments.

citations.excerpt: Definition 6. (1) An argument A ∈ AR is acceptable with respect to a set S of arguments iff for each argument B ∈ AR: if B attacks A then B is attacked by S. (2) A conflict-free set of arguments S is admissible iff each argument in S is acceptable with respect to S.

claims.statement: Dung defines acceptability: an argument A is acceptable with respect to a set S if every argument that attacks A is itself attacked by S; a conflict-free set S is admissible if each argument in S is acceptable with respect to S.

citations.excerpt: Definition 7. A preferred extension of an argumentation framework AF is a maximal (with respect to set inclusion) admissible set of AF.
Definition 13. A conflict-free set of arguments S is called a stable extension iff S attacks each argument which does not belong to S.
Definition 20. The grounded extension of an argumentation framework AF, denoted by GE_AF, is the least fixed point of F_AF.

claims.statement: Dung defines the preferred (credulous) extension as a maximal (by inclusion) admissible set; the grounded extension as the least fixed point of the characteristic function; and the stable extension as a conflict-free set that attacks every argument not in it.

citations.excerpt: Corollary 12. Every argumentation framework possesses at least one preferred extension.
The relations between stable extension and preferred extension are clarified in the following lemma. Lemma 15. Every stable extension is a preferred extension but not vice versa.
Example 22 ... The grounded extension is empty, i.e. a skeptical reasoner will not include anything.

claims.statement: Dung states that every argumentation framework has at least one preferred extension, but not every framework has a stable extension; the grounded extension may be empty, as in the Nixon diamond.

citations.excerpt: Definition 7. A preferred extension ... maximal admissible set

claims.statement: Design inference: In the Q/A graph, preferred extensions define credulous acceptance: an answer is credulously accepted if it belongs to at least one preferred extension of the current attack graph, allowing mutually inconsistent answers (each in different preferred extensions) to coexist as legitimate alternatives.

citations.excerpt: Definition 20. The grounded extension ... least fixed point
Example 22 ... a skeptical reasoner will not include anything.

claims.statement: Design inference: The grounded extension defines the skeptical set of answers: an answer is skeptically accepted (accepted regardless of conflict) exactly when it is in the grounded extension of the attack graph.

citations.excerpt: Definition 13. ... stable extension ... attacks each argument which does not belong to S.
Corollary 12 ... every argumentation framework possesses at least one preferred extension.

claims.statement: Design inference: Belief revision is modeled by mutating the attack relation (adding or removing conflict edges) or the set of arguments (adding or retracting answers) and then recomputing the extension(s) from the new framework; a stable extension, when present, can be used as the 'committed' revision outcome, but because stable extensions may not exist, the design must fall back on preferred (credulous) acceptance for revision that retains alternatives.

citations.excerpt: Theorem 52. ... the stable, well-founded and preferred extension semantics of P are in general incomputable.

claims.statement: Design inference: To keep revision tractable, the computation of extensions must be restricted to a finite, relevant subgraph (e.g., answers to a single question plus their transitive conflict closure), because Dung shows that in general the logic-programming semantics are incomputable; this is an architectural guardrail, not a source claim.

counterevidence: Source does not mention belief revision or graph substrate; any mapping to Q/A graph is inference, not source claim.
The source explicitly warns that stable semantics may not exist and that preferred extensions are not unique; the design must handle these as normal states.
The source's incomputability result (PDF PAGE 25) means that a naive 'recompute extensions over the whole graph' revision policy may be undecidable in the general case.
next_observation: To fully satisfy D8, I would need to confirm the runtime's update semantics (e.g., when revision is triggered) from sibling nodes or the parent's synthesis; I do not have that content here.
unresolved: I cannot cite any of the other six corpus files because their contents were not provided in this dossier; the design must therefore rely only on Dung's formalism for contradiction/revision.

The exact trigger semantics for when a revision is performed (e.g., new answer posted, conflict edge added, explicit user request) is not defined in this node; it is left to the runtime specification.

The treatment of weighted or typed conflicts (e.g., specificity vs. contradiction) is not addressed by Dung's binary attack relation; the source only mentions two kinds of attacks but not a formalization.
